pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, answered about their own project rather than in the abstract; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your suite is green and coverage is comfortably over the floor. What does that tell you, and what does it not? How would you find a line that is executed but not defended?
expected_points: coverage counts lines executed, not behaviour asserted — a test with no assertions scores the same
mutation thinking: change a line (< to <=, drop a return, return nil instead of err) and ask which test goes red
no test goes red means the line is covered but undefended
the usual gaps are error paths, boundaries, concurrent interleavings, and the seams between packages

questions.prompt: Where did you put a fuzz target in your project, and why there? What property does it assert, and what is the difference between the corpus you committed and the one in your build cache?
expected_points: target sits where untrusted bytes become a trusted value — parser, decoder, path/query/command builder
the property must hold for every input: no panic, accepted output satisfies the invariants, round trip is identity
seed corpus in testdata/fuzz/<Target>/ is committed and runs on every plain go test, everywhere
the generated corpus is machine-local, lives in the build cache, and is not shared
a crasher gets minimised and written to the seed corpus — commit it with the fix

questions.prompt: Walk me through the security pass on your own project: what were the trust boundaries, what did you check at each one, and what did the pass actually find?
expected_points: names concrete boundaries — stdin/args/files, network, environment, responses from peers
validation happens once at the boundary and produces a value the rest of the code can trust
OWASP categories that reach this size: injection into any interpreter (SQL, shell, path, URL), access control and defaults, secrets, resource exhaustion
a real finding rather than a hypothetical one; a systematic checklist rather than 'I read it over'

questions.prompt: Take the defect you fixed. Why write the failing test before the fix, and how do you know the test is any good?
expected_points: the test proves the defect is understood, and a fix aimed at the wrong cause shows up immediately
it gives 'is it fixed?' an answer that is not opinion
it stops the bug returning during a later refactor
you know it is good by watching it fail against the old code (stash the fix and run it)
named for the behaviour it defends, kept beside that package's other tests

questions.prompt: Why does an outbound HTTP client need a Timeout on the client itself, and why must a function that already receives a context.Context never call context.Background()?
expected_points: http.DefaultClient and http.Get/Post have no timeout — an unanswering peer pins the goroutine and connection forever
Client.Timeout bounds the whole exchange: connect, TLS, request, response headers and body
per-phase transport timeouts can all pass while the call still hangs
a fresh root context discards the caller's deadline, cancellation and values
roots belong in main/run; deliberate detachment is context.WithoutCancel plus a timeout of its own

questions.prompt: What does govulncheck tell you that a plain dependency scanner does not, and when does its answer stop being true?
expected_points: it reports reachability — a path from your code to the vulnerable symbol — not just 'you depend on an advisory'
that makes the output short enough to actually read
the answer expires on a toolchain upgrade (the standard library gets advisories too), on dependency changes, and on your own code changes that alter the call graph
run by hand, read every finding; grading is offline so no harness can run it for you

questions.prompt: Name something you chose not to harden. Convince me that was engineering rather than laziness.
expected_points: states the exposure concretely
states the reason, including the blast radius and the cost of fixing it
states the trigger that would reopen the decision
does not contradict a requirement in their own PRD
is written down in the security document, not just remembered

questions.prompt: Show me the top CPU and allocation entries you wrote down. Which surprised you, and why are you not fixing any of them today?
expected_points: produces the recorded top-N output, not a recollection — that file is the 'before' side of the next lesson's comparison
captured under a load defensible as realistic — sizes from the PRD, not ten items
can read the top entries: runtime.mallocgc/growslice means allocation in a loop; encoding/reflection means paying for convenience
surprises are the signal worth recording
optimising before the suite is trustworthy makes something fast and wrong; the measurement is kept for a later before/after comparison

questions.prompt: List every size limit in your project. Now name an input that has none — what does an attacker do with it?
expected_points: line/request length, decoded element counts, response bodies read from peers, slices allocated from a number in the input
without a limit the input decides how much memory the process uses
io.LimitReader, an explicit maximum constant, bufio.Scanner.Buffer; make([]T, n) with n from the wire is the anti-pattern
